claim: Neural representations of behaviorally relevant stimulus features displaying invariance with respect to different contexts are essential for perception.
source: Neural representations of behaviorally relevant stimulus features displaying invariance with respect to different contexts are essential for perception.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural representations and perception that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Correlated neural activity allows for the emergence of an invariant representation of natural communication stimuli in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
source: Here, we demonstrate that correlated neural activity allows for the emergence of an invariant representation of natural communication stimuli that is further refined across successive stages of processing in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from recordings at multiple processing stages.

claim: The invariant representation of natural communication stimuli is refined across successive stages of processing in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
source: Here, we demonstrate that correlated neural activity allows for the emergence of an invariant representation of natural communication stimuli that is further refined across successive stages of processing in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data showing increasing invariance scores across processing stages.

claim: Different patterns of input resulting from the same natural communication stimulus occurring in different contexts all gave rise to similar behavioral responses.
source: Importantly, different patterns of input resulting from the same natural communication stimulus occurring in different contexts all gave rise to similar behavioral responses.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing similar echo responses to different chirp waveforms.

claim: The invariant neural representation of natural stimuli constitutes a neural correlate of perception.
source: Our results thus reveal how a generic neural circuit performs an elegant computation that mediates the emergence and refinement of an invariant neural representation of natural stimuli that most likely constitutes a neural correlate of perception.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between neural invariance and behavioral invariance observed in the study.

claim: Neurons located in more central brain areas tend to respond more selectively to stimuli than neurons located in more peripheral brain areas.
source: Several studies have shown that neurons located in more central brain areas tend to respond more selectively to stimuli than neurons located in more peripheral brain areas (Rolls and Tovee, 1995; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Hromadka et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neural representations in more central brain areas become more robust to the differential patterns of sensory input associated with a given stimulus.
source: At the same time, however, neural representations in more central brain areas become more robust to the differential patterns of sensory input associated with a given stimulus (e.g. those experienced when looking at the same object under different levels of illumination).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field with an example provided.

claim: Invariant representations are thought to mediate context-independent object recognition.
source: Such invariant representations are thought to mediate context-independent object recognition and have been observed across sensory modalities (auditory: [Bendor and Wang, 2005; Barbour, 2011; Bizley and Cohen, 2013; Rabinowitz et al., 2013]; visual: [Quiroga et al., 2005; Zoccolan et al., 2007; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Sharpee et al., 2013]; somatosensory: [DiCarlo and Johnson, 1999; Pei et al., 2010]; olfactory: [Stopfer et al., 2003; Cleland et al., 2007]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies across multiple sensory modalities.

claim: Invariant representations have been observed across sensory modalities including auditory, visual, somatosensory, and olfactory systems.
source: Such invariant representations are thought to mediate context-independent object recognition and have been observed across sensory modalities (auditory: [Bendor and Wang, 2005; Barbour, 2011; Bizley and Cohen, 2013; Rabinowitz et al., 2013]; visual: [Quiroga et al., 2005; Zoccolan et al., 2007; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Sharpee et al., 2013]; somatosensory: [DiCarlo and Johnson, 1999; Pei et al., 2010]; olfactory: [Stopfer et al., 2003; Cleland et al., 2007]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in different sensory systems.

claim: Modeling studies have proposed that invariant representations are built and refined in a feedforward manner across successive brain areas by using OR-like operations.
source: Modeling studies have proposed that such representations are built and refined in a feedforward manner across successive brain areas by using OR-like operations (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Kouh and Poggio, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Combining neural activities that are locally invariant to complementary subsets of stimulus waveforms associated with a given object should give rise to a more globally invariant representation.
source: Indeed, these studies suggest that combining neural activities that are locally invariant to complementary subsets of stimulus waveforms associated with a given object should then give rise to a more globally invariant representation.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from modeling studies.

claim: The actual computations used by the brain that give rise to invariant neural representations remain poorly understood.
source: However, the actual computations used by the brain that give rise to invariant neural representations remain poorly understood to this day.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Wave-type gymnotiform weakly electric fish offer an attractive model system for studying the emergence and refinement of feature invariant neural representations.
source: Wave-type gymnotiform weakly electric fish offer an attractive model system for studying the emergence and refinement of feature invariant neural representations because of well-characterized anatomy and relatively simple natural sensory stimuli that can easily be mimicked in the laboratory (Chacron et al., 2011; Marsat et al., 2012; Marquez et al., 2013; Stamper et al., 2013; Krahe and Maler, 2014; Clarke et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work characterizing this model system.

claim: Weakly electric fish have well-characterized anatomy.
source: Wave-type gymnotiform weakly electric fish offer an attractive model system for studying the emergence and refinement of feature invariant neural representations because of well-characterized anatomy and relatively simple natural sensory stimuli that can easily be mimicked in the laboratory (Chacron et al., 2011; Marsat et al., 2012; Marquez et al., 2013; Stamper et al., 2013; Krahe and Maler, 2014; Clarke et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Weakly electric fish have relatively simple natural sensory stimuli that can easily be mimicked in the laboratory.
source: Wave-type gymnotiform weakly electric fish offer an attractive model system for studying the emergence and refinement of feature invariant neural representations because of well-characterized anatomy and relatively simple natural sensory stimuli that can easily be mimicked in the laboratory (Chacron et al., 2011; Marsat et al., 2012; Marquez et al., 2013; Stamper et al., 2013; Krahe and Maler, 2014; Clarke et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and demonstrated by the experimental approach in this study.

claim: Weakly electric fish generate a quasi-sinusoidal electric organ discharge (EOD) at a typical individual frequency.
source: These fish generate a quasi-sinusoidal electric organ discharge (EOD) at a typical individual frequency, resulting in an electric field that surrounds the body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biology of weakly electric fish.

claim: The EOD of weakly electric fish results in an electric field that surrounds the body.
source: These fish generate a quasi-sinusoidal electric organ discharge (EOD) at a typical individual frequency, resulting in an electric field that surrounds the body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biology of weakly electric fish.

claim: EOD perturbations are sensed by an array of electroreceptors that synapse onto pyramidal neurons within the hindbrain electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL).
source: EOD perturbations are sensed by an array of electroreceptors that synapse onto pyramidal neurons within the hindbrain electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL) that in turn synapse onto neurons within the midbrain Torus semicircularis (TS).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the electrosensory system.

claim: ELL pyramidal neurons synapse onto neurons within the midbrain Torus semicircularis (TS).
source: EOD perturbations are sensed by an array of electroreceptors that synapse onto pyramidal neurons within the hindbrain electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL) that in turn synapse onto neurons within the midbrain Torus semicircularis (TS).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the electrosensory system.

claim: When two conspecifics come into contact (<1 m), each fish experiences a sinusoidal amplitude modulation (i.e. beat) with a frequency that is equal to the difference between the two EOD frequencies.
source: When two conspecifics come into contact (<1 m), each fish experiences a sinusoidal amplitude modulation (i.e. beat) with a frequency that is equal to the difference between the two EOD frequencies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physics of EOD interference.

claim: Natural communication signals or chirps consist of transient increases in EOD frequency.
source: Natural communication signals or chirps consist of transient increases in EOD frequency and always occur simultaneously with the beat under natural conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the behavior of weakly electric fish.

claim: Chirps always occur simultaneously with the beat under natural conditions.
source: Natural communication signals or chirps consist of transient increases in EOD frequency and always occur simultaneously with the beat under natural conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the natural context of chirp signals.

claim: Stimulus waveforms associated with chirps can be uniquely characterized by the increase in EOD frequency, duration, and the beat phase at onset.
source: Stimulus waveforms associated with chirps can be uniquely characterized by the increase in EOD frequency, duration, and the beat phase at onset.
evidence: This is a characterization of chirp stimuli based on established knowledge and used in the experimental design.

claim: Chirp stimulus waveforms are highly heterogeneous.
source: It has long been recognized that chirp stimulus waveforms are highly heterogeneous (Zupanc and Maler, 1993; Hupé and lewis., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Duration and frequency increase of chirps are both narrowly distributed.
source: Interestingly, a recent study has shown that, while duration and frequency increase of chirps were both narrowly distributed, the beat phase at chirp onset was instead uniformly distributed over the entire beat cycle (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The beat phase at chirp onset is uniformly distributed over the entire beat cycle.
source: Interestingly, a recent study has shown that, while duration and frequency increase of chirps were both narrowly distributed, the beat phase at chirp onset was instead uniformly distributed over the entire beat cycle (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The observed heterogeneities in stimulus waveforms are, at least in part, caused by the fact that a chirp with given frequency increase and duration can occur with equal probability at any phase of the beat cycle.
source: This suggests that the observed heterogeneities in stimulus waveforms are, at least in part, caused by the fact that a chirp with given frequency increase and duration can occur with equal probability at any phase of the beat cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study showing uniform distribution of beat phase at chirp onset.

claim: Weakly electric fish perceive chirps as evidenced from behavioral responses.
source: Previous studies have shown that weakly electric fish perceive chirps as evidenced from behavioral responses (Hupé and Lewis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous behavioral study.

claim: Both afferents and ELL pyramidal neurons tend to respond differentially to different chirp stimulus waveforms.
source: Electrophysiological studies have also characterized how chirps are encoded across successive stages of processing and notably, both afferents and ELL pyramidal neurons tend to respond differentially to different chirp stimulus waveforms (Benda et al., 2005; 2006; Marsat et al., 2009; Marsat and Maler, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: TS neurons display large heterogeneities in their responses to chirps.
source: TS neurons display large heterogeneities in their responses: while some respond in a manner that is similar to that of ELL neurons, others instead respond selectively to chirps through reliable and precisely timed action potentials (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Some TS neurons respond in a manner that is similar to that of ELL neurons.
source: TS neurons display large heterogeneities in their responses: while some respond in a manner that is similar to that of ELL neurons, others instead respond selectively to chirps through reliable and precisely timed action potentials (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Some TS neurons respond selectively to chirps through reliable and precisely timed action potentials.
source: TS neurons display large heterogeneities in their responses: while some respond in a manner that is similar to that of ELL neurons, others instead respond selectively to chirps through reliable and precisely timed action potentials (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Some TS neurons can respond similarly to different chirp stimulus waveforms.
source: A recent study has, furthermore, shown that some TS neurons can respond similarly to different chirp stimulus waveforms (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: In the absence of communication signals, interference between the emitter and receiver fish's EODs gives rise to a sinusoidal amplitude modulation (the beat).
source: In the absence of communication signals (i.e. when both EOD frequencies are constant), interference between the emitter and receiver fish's EODs gives rise to a sinusoidal amplitude modulation as mentioned above (i.e. the beat) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Natural communication stimuli (chirps) occur during social interactions in which the emitter fish sends the signal to the receiver fish.
source: Natural communication stimuli (i.e. chirps) occur during social interactions in which the emitter fish sends the signal to the receiver fish (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the behavioral context of chirps, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The chirp consists of one fish increasing its EOD frequency for a short duration.
source: The chirp consists of one fish increasing its EOD frequency for a short duration (Figure 1D, top red/green trace), which, when considering the resulting stimulus sensed by the receiver fish, consists of a transient perturbation of the underlying beat (Figure 1D, black bottom trace).
evidence: This is a description of the chirp signal illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: When considering the resulting stimulus sensed by the receiver fish, a chirp consists of a transient perturbation of the underlying beat.
source: The chirp consists of one fish increasing its EOD frequency for a short duration (Figure 1D, top red/green trace), which, when considering the resulting stimulus sensed by the receiver fish, consists of a transient perturbation of the underlying beat (Figure 1D, black bottom trace).
evidence: This is a description of how the chirp is perceived by the receiver, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: A chirp with a given EOD frequency timecourse can occur with uniform probability at all phases of the beat.
source: Because a chirp with a given EOD frequency timecourse (i.e. 'identity') can occur with uniform probability at all phases of the beat (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015), the resulting stimulus waveforms display significant heterogeneities (Figure 1E, gray bands, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The resulting stimulus waveforms display significant heterogeneities when a chirp occurs at different phases of the beat.
source: Because a chirp with a given EOD frequency timecourse (i.e. 'identity') can occur with uniform probability at all phases of the beat (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015), the resulting stimulus waveforms display significant heterogeneities (Figure 1E, gray bands, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single peripheral receptor afferents display minimal phase invariance.
source: We first recorded from single peripheral receptor afferents (Figure 2A) in response to different patterns of sensory input resulting from the same chirp stimulus occurring at different phases during the beat cycle (Figure 1E). Single afferent responses consisted of patterns of excitation and inhibition that strongly depended on the stimulus waveform that was presented (Figure 2B, blue curves).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Single afferent responses consisted of patterns of excitation and inhibition that strongly depended on the stimulus waveform that was presented.
source: Single afferent responses consisted of patterns of excitation and inhibition that strongly depended on the stimulus waveform that was presented (Figure 2B, blue curves).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 2B.

claim: Population-averaged responses of afferents strongly varied depending on where the chirp occurred within the beat cycle.
source: Indeed, population-averaged responses strongly varied depending on where the chirp occurred within the beat cycle (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 2C.

claim: Afferents were excited when the chirp occurred at beat phases lower than 180°.
source: Afferents were excited when the chirp occurred at beat phases lower than 180° and inhibited when it occurred at beat phases greater or equal to 180° (Figure 2D, blue curve).
evidence: This is shown in the tuning curve data in Figure 2D.

claim: Afferents were inhibited when the chirp occurred at beat phases greater or equal to 180°.
source: Afferents were excited when the chirp occurred at beat phases lower than 180° and inhibited when it occurred at beat phases greater or equal to 180° (Figure 2D, blue curve).
evidence: This is shown in the tuning curve data in Figure 2D.

claim: The invariance score for single afferents was near zero (mean: 0.11 ± 0.01; max: 0.15; min: 0.07; population: 0.08).
source: We found that the invariance score for single afferents was near zero (mean: 0.11 ± 0.01; max: 0.15; min: 0.07; population: 0.08) (Figure 2E, inset): this is because the distance between responses was always more or less equal to the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The distance between responses of single afferents was always more or less equal to the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms.
source: We found that the invariance score for single afferents was near zero (mean: 0.11 ± 0.01; max: 0.15; min: 0.07; population: 0.08) (Figure 2E, inset): this is because the distance between responses was always more or less equal to the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The low invariance value for single afferents was not due to variability in the response of single afferents.
source: We note that this low value was not due to variability in the response of single afferents, as the population responses obtained by linearly summating the individual neural responses also displayed invariance scores near zero (Figure 2E, inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing single neuron and population invariance scores in Figure 2E.

claim: Population responses obtained by linearly summating the individual neural responses also displayed invariance scores near zero.
source: We note that this low value was not due to variability in the response of single afferents, as the population responses obtained by linearly summating the individual neural responses also displayed invariance scores near zero (Figure 2E, inset).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 2E inset.

claim: Computing invariance scores using only responses to subsets of chirps (same type '++/- -' or opposite type '+-' chirp combinations) resulted in low values for single afferents.
source: We further note that computing invariance scores using only responses to subsets of chirps (i.e. those computed using only same type '++/- -' or opposite type '+-' chirp combinations) resulted in low values as well (Figure 2F, blue).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 2F.

claim: Single peripheral afferent responses faithfully encoded the different patterns of sensory input resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within the beat cycle.
source: Thus, we conclude that single peripheral afferent responses were minimally phase invariant as these neurons faithfully encoded the different patterns of sensory input resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within the beat cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the invariance score data.

claim: Afferent activities were always more similar after chirp onset as afferent spiking activities were more synchronized either through excitation or inhibition.
source: Similar results were seen when considering simultaneously recorded or recombined pairs: afferent activities were always more similar after chirp onset as afferent spiking activities were more synchronized either through excitation or inhibition (Figure 2B, blue curves compare Firing Rate 1 to Firing Rate 2).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 2B comparing firing rates.

claim: Correlation transiently increased following chirp onset in afferent pairs.
source: Our results show that correlation transiently increased following chirp onset (Figure 2B, purple curves).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation data in Figure 2B.

claim: The time course of the correlation coefficient was similar for all stimulus waveforms in afferent pairs.
source: Importantly, the time course of the correlation coefficient was similar for all stimulus waveforms (Figure 2E), as quantified by a large invariance score (mean: 0.53 ± 0.02; max: 0.67; min: 0.35; population: 0.61) (Figure 2E, inset & Figure 2F)
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 2E and quantified by the invariance score.

claim: Correlated afferent activity has a large invariance score (mean: 0.53 ± 0.02; max: 0.67; min: 0.35; population: 0.61).
source: Importantly, the time course of the correlation coefficient was similar for all stimulus waveforms (Figure 2E), as quantified by a large invariance score (mean: 0.53 ± 0.02; max: 0.67; min: 0.35; population: 0.61) (Figure 2E, inset & Figure 2F)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: The invariance score for correlated activity was not significantly different for simultaneously recorded (0.51 ± 0.02) or recombined (0.53 ± 0.03) afferent activities (t-test, p=0.4).
source: that was not significantly different for either simultaneously recorded (0.51 ± 0.02) or recombined (0.53 ± 0.03) afferent activities (t-test, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the data.

claim: The high invariance scores for correlated activity were obtained because the distance between the time-varying correlation coefficient was always less than that between the corresponding stimulus waveforms.
source: These high invariance scores were obtained because the distance between the time-varying correlation coefficient was always less than that between the corresponding stimulus waveforms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar results for correlated activity invariance were observed when systematically varying the time scale at which correlations were computed up to ∼60 ms.
source: Similar results were observed when systematically varying the time scale at which correlations were computed up to ∼60 ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Correlated activity at short timescales in receptor afferents displays phase invariance.
source: We conclude that correlated activity at short timescales in receptor afferents displays phase invariance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the invariance score data for correlated activity.

claim: ELL pyramidal neurons receive synaptic input from afferents.
source: To investigate whether the electrosensory system actually uses the fact that correlated afferent activity provides a phase invariant representation of natural communication signals, we recorded from hindbrain ELL pyramidal neurons (Figure 3A). These receive synaptic input from afferents and furthermore constitute the sole output neurons of the ELL (Maler, 1979; Maler et al., 1981).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ELL pyramidal neurons constitute the sole output neurons of the ELL.
source: These receive synaptic input from afferents and furthermore constitute the sole output neurons of the ELL (Maler, 1979; Maler et al., 1981).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pyramidal neurons can be classified as either ON or OFF-type based on whether they respond to increases in stimulus amplitude through increases or decreases in firing rate, respectively.
source: Pyramidal neurons can be classified as either ON or OFF-type based on whether they respond to increases in stimulus amplitude through increases or decreases in firing rate, respectively (Saunders and Bastian, 1984) (see [Clarke et al., 2015b] for review).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pyramidal neuron classification supported by citations.

claim: Pyramidal neurons respond to correlated afferent activity.
source: Previous results have shown that pyramidal neurons respond to correlated afferent activity (Berman and Maler, 1999; Middleton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ON-type ELL pyramidal neurons display significantly more phase invariance than single afferents.
source: Consistent with our predictions, ELL pyramidal neurons were significantly more phase invariant than single afferents (ELL ON; mean: 0.19 ± 0.01; max: 0.32; min: 0.03; population: 0.19; ELL OFF; mean: 0.16 ± 0.01; max: 0.21; min: 0.07; population: 0.16) (ANOVA with Bonferroni correction, p<0.01) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical comparison of the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons display significantly more phase invariance than single afferents.
source: Consistent with our predictions, ELL pyramidal neurons were significantly more phase invariant than single afferents (ELL ON; mean: 0.19 ± 0.01; max: 0.32; min: 0.03; population: 0.19; ELL OFF; mean: 0.16 ± 0.01; max: 0.21; min: 0.07; population: 0.16) (ANOVA with Bonferroni correction, p<0.01) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical comparison of the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: '+ chirps' mostly gave rise to similar excitatory activity patterns in ON-type cells.
source: Our results were largely consistent with these predictions as '+ chirps' mostly gave rise to similar excitatory activity patterns in ON-type cells (Figure 3B, top rows, green; Figure 3C, dark green)
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: '+ chirps' mostly gave rise to inhibitory activity patterns in OFF-type cells.
source: Our results were largely consistent with these predictions as '+ chirps' mostly gave rise to similar excitatory activity patterns in ON-type cells (Figure 3B, top rows, green; Figure 3C, dark green) and inhibitory activity patterns in OFF-type cells (Figure 3B, top rows, magenta; Figure 3D, light magenta).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: '- chirps' mostly gave rise to patterns of inhibition in ON-type cells.
source: In contrast, '- chirps' mostly gave rise to patterns of inhibition in ON-type cells (Figure 3B, lower rows, green; Figure 3C, light green)
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: '- chirps' mostly gave rise to excitation in OFF-type cells.
source: In contrast, '- chirps' mostly gave rise to patterns of inhibition in ON-type cells (Figure 3B, lower rows, green; Figure 3C, light green) and excitation in OFF-type cells (Figure 3B, lower rows, magenta; Figure 3D, dark magenta).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: The population responses of ON and OFF cells were negatively correlated during responses to all waveforms.
source: The complementarity of responses was furthermore reflected by the fact that the population responses of ON and OFF cells were negatively correlated during responses to all waveforms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average tuning curves of ON and OFF-type cells were mirror images of one another.
source: Consequently, the average tuning curves of ON and OFF-type cells were mirror images of one another (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 3E.

claim: The distance between responses of ELL pyramidal neurons was, on average, lower than that between the corresponding stimulus waveforms.
source: Further analysis revealed that this was because the distance between responses was, on average, lower than that between the corresponding stimulus waveforms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Invariance scores computed for same-type chirp combinations were significantly larger than those computed for opposite-type chirp combinations for both ON (ANOVA; p<0.01) and OFF-type (ANOVA; p<0.018) pyramidal cells.
source: We found that invariance scores computed for same-type chirp combinations were significantly larger than those computed for opposite-type chirp combinations for both ON (ANOVA; p<0.01) and OFF-type (ANOVA; p<0.018) pyramidal cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Average invariance score values computed for opposite-type chirp combinations in ON (0.15 ± 0.02) and OFF-type (0.11 ± 0.01) ELL pyramidal cells were similar to those obtained for single afferents (0.16 ± 0.002).
source: Further, average invariance score values computed for opposite-type chirp combinations in ON (0.15 ± 0.02) and OFF-type (0.11 ± 0.01) ELL pyramidal cells were similar to those obtained for single afferents (0.16 ± 0.002) (compare Figures 3F and 2F).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative results across different cell types.

claim: The increased phase invariance of ELL pyramidal cells is due to the fact that they respond more similarly to '+ chirps' and '- chirps' than single afferents.
source: These results thus confirm our hypothesis that the increased phase invariance of ELL pyramidal cells is due to the fact that they respond more similarly to '+ chirps' and '- chirps' than single afferents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of invariance scores for different chirp combinations.

claim: Phase invariance in ELL is limited by the fact that ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells both respond in opposite fashion to different subsets of chirp stimulus waveforms.
source: However, phase invariance in ELL is limited by the fact that ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells both respond in opposite fashion to different subsets of chirp stimulus waveforms (i.e. '+ chirps' and '- chirps').
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of responses to different chirp types.

claim: Neurons within the midbrain TS receive only direct excitatory synaptic input from multiple ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons.
source: Anatomical studies have shown that neurons within the midbrain TS receive only direct excitatory synaptic input from multiple ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons (Carr and Maler, 1985), as reflected by their response properties (McGillivray et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TS neurons responded with excitation to most stimulus waveforms.
source: Our results show that TS neurons indeed responded with excitation to most stimulus waveforms (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 4B.

claim: TS neuron responses were more similar than those of either single afferents or ELL pyramidal neurons.
source: Our results show that TS neurons indeed responded with excitation to most stimulus waveforms (Figure 4B) and that, consequently, responses were more similar than those of either single afferents or ELL pyramidal neurons (compare Figure 4C with Figures 3C,D, and 2C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing data across Figures 2C, 3C, 3D, and 4C.

claim: The phase invariance score of TS neurons (mean: 0.26 ± 0.02; max: 0.49; min: 0.16; population: 0.4) was significantly higher than that of ELL neurons (ANOVA with Bonferroni correction, p<0.01) when considering all waveforms.
source: The response similarity was reflected in the population-averaged tuning curves (Figure 4D) as well as in the phase invariance score (mean: 0.26 ± 0.02; max: 0.49; min: 0.16; population: 0.4) that was significantly higher than that of ELL neurons (ANOVA with Bonferroni correction, p<0.01) when considering all waveforms (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The distance between responses of TS neurons is considerably lower than the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms.
source: This is because the distance between responses is considerably lower than the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phase invariance score values obtained for the TS neuron population (0.4) approached those observed for correlated peripheral afferent activity (0.53).
source: Phase invariance score values obtained for the TS neuron population (0.4) furthermore approached those observed for correlated peripheral afferent activity (0.53).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative results.

claim: The population-averaged response of TS neurons decreased for '- chirps'.
source: We note that the population-averaged response of TS neurons decreased for '- chirps' (Figure 4D): this is because some TS neurons responded similarly to ELL ON-type pyramidal cells and were thus inhibited by '- chirps'.
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 4D and explained by the heterogeneity of TS neurons.

claim: Some TS neurons responded similarly to ELL ON-type pyramidal cells and were thus inhibited by '- chirps'.
source: We note that the population-averaged response of TS neurons decreased for '- chirps' (Figure 4D): this is because some TS neurons responded similarly to ELL ON-type pyramidal cells and were thus inhibited by '- chirps'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed response patterns.

claim: TS neurons with larger phase invariance scores (N=13) were excited by all chirp waveforms as quantified by positive responses for all chirp waveforms.
source: However, TS neurons with larger phase invariance scores (N=13) were excited by all chirp waveforms as quantified by positive responses for all chirp waveforms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Computing phase invariance scores over either same type ('++/- -') or opposite type ('+-') chirp combinations led to values that were not significantly different from one another (++/- -: 0.24 ± 0.02; +-: 0.28 ± 0.02) (ANOVA; F = 1.3, p=0.28) for TS neurons.
source: Further, computing phase invariance scores over either same type ('++/- -') or opposite type ('+-') chirp combinations led to values that were not significantly different from one another (++/- -: 0.24 ± 0.02; +-: 0.28 ± 0.02) (ANOVA; F = 1.3, p=0.28) and that were furthermore similar to those obtained using all waveforms (0.26 ± 0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the data.

claim: TS neurons are, on average, more phase invariant than ELL pyramidal cells because a significant fraction (∼50%) responds with excitation to both '+ chirps' and '- chirps'.
source: This confirms our hypothesis that TS neurons are, on average, more phase invariant than ELL pyramidal cells because a significant fraction (∼50%) responds with excitation to both '+ chirps' and '- chirps'.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of TS neuron responses.

claim: The simplest explanation for TS neurons responding to both '+ chirps' and '- chirps' is that these neurons receive excitatory input from ELL ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells.
source: The simplest explanation for this observation is that these neurons receive excitatory input from ELL ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy and observed response patterns.

claim: The elicited behavioral responses to different chirp waveforms were very similar.
source: If our hypothesis is true, then we expect that all the presented waveforms will elicit similar behavioral responses. Confirming our hypothesis, the elicited behavioral responses were very similar (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The behavioral response tuning was effectively independent of beat phase.
source: Consequently, the response tuning was effectively independent of beat phase (Figure 5E, top).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral tuning curve in Figure 5E.

claim: Response latency and rate of occurrence did not depend on beat phase.
source: Importantly, other measures such as response latency and rate of occurrence also did not depend on beat phase (Figure 5E, bottom).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 5E.

claim: Invariance values computed from behavioral responses were near unity.
source: Invariance values computed from behavioral responses were near unity (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 5F.

claim: The distance between behavioral responses is considerably lower than the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms.
source: This is because the distance between responses is considerably lower than the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organism perceives the different patterns of stimulation input resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within the beat cycle in a similar fashion and thus displays perceptual phase invariance.
source: We conclude that the organism perceives the different patterns of stimulation input resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within the beat cycle in a similar fashion and thus displays perceptual phase invariance
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing similar responses to different waveforms.

claim: Correlated but not single afferent activity provided a phase invariant representation of natural communication stimuli.
source: So far, we have shown that correlated but not single afferent activity provided a phase invariant representation of natural communication stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the afferent recordings.

claim: ELL pyramidal neurons responded primarily through excitation to one half of the input patterns resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within the beat cycle and through inhibition to the other half, which limits phase invariance.
source: Recordings from ELL pyramidal neurons revealed that these responded primarily through excitation to one half of the input patterns resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within the beat cycle and through inhibition to the other half, which limits phase invariance.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the ELL recordings.

claim: The tuning curves became progressively more independent of beat phase when comparing peripheral afferents, ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons, TS neurons, and behavior.
source: The tuning curves became progressively more independent of beat phase when comparing peripheral afferents, ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons, TS neurons, and behavior (Figure 6B), thereby leading to increased levels of phase invariance (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in the summary data in Figure 6B.

claim: Phase invariance progressively increases across successive stages of electrosensory processing as well as behavior.
source: The tuning curves became progressively more independent of beat phase when comparing peripheral afferents, ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons, TS neurons, and behavior (Figure 6B), thereby leading to increased levels of phase invariance (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in the summary data in Figure 6C.

claim: The responses of single peripheral afferents displayed minimal phase invariance, as these neurons faithfully encoded all the different waveforms resulting from the same chirp stimulus occurring at different phases within the beat cycle.
source: We found that the responses of single peripheral afferents displayed minimal phase invariance, as these neurons faithfully encoded all the different waveforms resulting from the same chirp stimulus occurring at different phases within the beat cycle.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the afferent recordings.

claim: Simultaneous recordings from afferent pairs revealed that these waveforms all gave rise to similar increases in correlated activity.
source: In contrast, simultaneous recordings from afferent pairs revealed that these waveforms all gave rise to similar increases in correlated activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the paired afferent recordings.

claim: ON and OFF-type ELL neurons displayed significantly higher phase invariance than single peripheral afferents.
source: ON and OFF-type ELL neurons displayed significantly higher phase invariance than single peripheral afferents.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the ELL recordings.

claim: Both the ON and OFF-type subpopulations showed the greatest degree of phase invariance to waveforms giving rise to either excitation or inhibition in afferents.
source: Indeed, both the ON and OFF-type subpopulations showed the greatest degree of phase invariance to waveforms giving rise to either excitation or inhibition in afferents.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the ELL recordings.

claim: Responses from both ON and OFF subpopulations are most likely combined in the midbrain TS, thereby giving rise to a more phase invariant representation.
source: Responses from both subpopulations are most likely combined in the midbrain TS, thereby giving rise to a more phase invariant representation that, at the population level, approached that seen for correlated afferent activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy and observed response patterns.

claim: The phase invariant representation observed in midbrain at the population level approached that seen for correlated afferent activity.
source: Responses from both subpopulations are most likely combined in the midbrain TS, thereby giving rise to a more phase invariant representation that, at the population level, approached that seen for correlated afferent activity.
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative results.

claim: Weakly electric fish displayed similar behavioral responses to stimulus waveforms generated by applying an identity-preserving transformation.
source: Finally, we showed that weakly electric fish displayed similar behavioral responses to stimulus waveforms generated by applying an identity-preserving transformation, which strongly suggests that the globally invariant representation observed in midbrain constitutes a neural correlate of perception.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: The globally invariant representation observed in midbrain constitutes a neural correlate of perception.
source: Finally, we showed that weakly electric fish displayed similar behavioral responses to stimulus waveforms generated by applying an identity-preserving transformation, which strongly suggests that the globally invariant representation observed in midbrain constitutes a neural correlate of perception.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between neural invariance and behavioral invariance.

claim: Single peripheral afferents and ELL pyramidal neurons display differential responses to heterogeneous natural communication stimulus waveforms.
source: Previous studies have reported that the waveforms associated with natural communication stimuli were highly heterogeneous with respect to their time course (Zupanc and Maler, 1993) and that single peripheral afferents (Benda et al., 2005, 2006) as well as ELL pyramidal neurons (Marsat et al., 2009; Marsat and Maler, 2010; Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011) display differential responses to these.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The different waveforms resulting from a chirp with given frequency increase and duration occurring at different phases within the beat cycle tend to give rise to more similar neural responses centrally.
source: Our results show that the different waveforms resulting from a chirp with given frequency increase and duration occurring at different phases within the beat cycle tend to give rise to more similar neural responses centrally.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The more similar neural responses centrally most likely constitute a neural correlate of perception.
source: Our results show that the different waveforms resulting from a chirp with given frequency increase and duration occurring at different phases within the beat cycle tend to give rise to more similar neural responses centrally. These most likely constitute a neural correlate of perception.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between neural and behavioral invariance.

claim: The electrophysiological and behavioral results support the hypothesis that the identity of a given chirp is determined by frequency increase and duration but not the phase of the beat at which it occurs.
source: Our electrophysiological and behavioral results thus support our initial hypothesis that the identity of a given chirp is determined by frequency increase and duration but not the phase of the beat at which it occurs at.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined neural and behavioral data.

claim: TS neurons displayed significantly less phase invariance than behavioral responses, indicating that further refinement in downstream brain areas is likely necessary.
source: Our results further show that TS neurons displayed significantly less phase invariance than behavioral responses, indicating that further refinement in downstream brain areas is likely necessary.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of TS neuron and behavioral invariance scores.

claim: Refinement of phase invariance is likely to occur in the nucleus electrosensorius, a diencephalic brain structure that receives direct input from TS.
source: Such refinement is likely to occur in the nucleus electrosensorius, a diencephalic brain structure that receives direct input from TS (Carr et al., 1981), and likely involves integrating the activities of multiple TS neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known anatomy and the observed gap between TS and behavioral invariance.

claim: Refinement of phase invariance likely involves integrating the activities of multiple TS neurons.
source: Such refinement is likely to occur in the nucleus electrosensorius, a diencephalic brain structure that receives direct input from TS (Carr et al., 1981), and likely involves integrating the activities of multiple TS neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that population invariance is higher than single neuron invariance.

claim: The fact that the invariance score of the TS neuron population was on average higher than that of single neurons supports the statement that refinement involves integrating the activities of multiple TS neurons.
source: The fact that the invariance score of the TS neuron population was on average higher than that of single neurons supports the latter statement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of single neuron and population invariance scores.

claim: The TS in weakly electric fish consists of 11 layers with roughly 50 cell types.
source: Importantly, we note here that the TS in weakly electric fish consists of 11 layers with roughly 50 cell types (Carr and Maler, 1985).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TS neurons are highly heterogeneous and can be roughly classified in two groups: 'dense' neurons and 'sparse' neurons.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies have revealed that TS neurons are highly heterogeneous and can be roughly classified in two groups: 'dense' neurons that respond to stimuli in a manner that is strongly reminiscent of that displayed by ELL pyramidal neurons; and 'sparse' neurons that respond selectively to a given class of natural electrosensory stimuli (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011; Sproule et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 'Dense' TS neurons respond to stimuli in a manner that is strongly reminiscent of that displayed by ELL pyramidal neurons.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies have revealed that TS neurons are highly heterogeneous and can be roughly classified in two groups: 'dense' neurons that respond to stimuli in a manner that is strongly reminiscent of that displayed by ELL pyramidal neurons; and 'sparse' neurons that respond selectively to a given class of natural electrosensory stimuli (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011; Sproule et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 'Sparse' TS neurons respond selectively to a given class of natural electrosensory stimuli.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies have revealed that TS neurons are highly heterogeneous and can be roughly classified in two groups: 'dense' neurons that respond to stimuli in a manner that is strongly reminiscent of that displayed by ELL pyramidal neurons; and 'sparse' neurons that respond selectively to a given class of natural electrosensory stimuli (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011; Sproule et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Within the sparse group, neurons can either respond selectively to movement, increases in beat amplitude (envelopes), or natural communication stimuli.
source: Within the sparse group, neurons can either respond selectively to movement (Chacron et al., 2009; Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011), increases in beat amplitude (i.e. envelopes) (McGillivray et al., 2012), or natural communication stimuli (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011), indicating that parallel processing of behaviorally relevant stimulus features occurs in this area.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Parallel processing of behaviorally relevant stimulus features occurs in the TS.
source: Within the sparse group, neurons can either respond selectively to movement (Chacron et al., 2009; Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011), increases in beat amplitude (i.e. envelopes) (McGillivray et al., 2012), or natural communication stimuli (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011), indicating that parallel processing of behaviorally relevant stimulus features occurs in this area.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of selective responses observed in TS neurons.

claim: Some TS neurons displayed phase invariance scores that were higher than those observed in single receptors or in ELL neurons.
source: Interestingly, some TS neurons displayed phase invariance scores that were higher than those observed in single receptors or in ELL neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the TS recordings.

claim: TS neurons with high phase invariance are likely members of the sparse group as they responded selectively to communication stimuli rather than the underlying beat.
source: It is likely that these are members of the sparse group as they responded selectively to communication stimuli rather than the underlying beat.
evidence: This is an inference based on the response properties and previous classifications.

claim: Some TS neurons with similar response profiles receive balanced excitatory input from ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells.
source: A previous study has shown that neurons with similar response profiles receive balanced excitatory input from ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015) and, as such, most likely correspond to previously described 'ON-OFF' neurons that respond to both increases and decreases in the stimulus (Partridge et al., 1981; Rose and Call, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some TS neurons most likely correspond to previously described 'ON-OFF' neurons that respond to both increases and decreases in the stimulus.
source: A previous study has shown that neurons with similar response profiles receive balanced excitatory input from ON and OFF-type pyramidal cells (Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015) and, as such, most likely correspond to previously described 'ON-OFF' neurons that respond to both increases and decreases in the stimulus (Partridge et al., 1981; Rose and Call, 1993).
evidence: This is an inference based on the response properties and supported by citations.

claim: ON-OFF neurons correspond to a few if not a single cell type within TS.
source: We, however, note that these neurons correspond to a few if not a single cell type within TS (Carr et al., 1981; Carr and Maler, 1985), as partially reflected by the broad distribution of phase invariance scores observed in the current study in TS neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies and the observed distribution of invariance scores.

claim: A significant fraction of TS neurons displayed low-phase invariance scores comparable to those seen in ELL.
source: In fact, confirming previous results (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011), a significant fraction of TS neurons displayed low-phase invariance scores comparable to those seen in ELL, indicating that they responded differentially (i.e. non-invariantly) to the different waveforms resulting from a given chirp occurring at different phases within the cycle of a beat.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the TS recordings, supported by citation.

claim: Both dense and sparse TS neurons project to higher brain areas.
source: Interestingly, it was shown recently that both dense and sparse TS neurons project to higher brain areas (Sproule et al., 2015), indicating that these actually receive parallel sources of information including those transmitted by both phase invariant and non-phase invariant TS neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Higher brain areas receive parallel sources of information including those transmitted by both phase invariant and non-phase invariant TS neurons.
source: Interestingly, it was shown recently that both dense and sparse TS neurons project to higher brain areas (Sproule et al., 2015), indicating that these actually receive parallel sources of information including those transmitted by both phase invariant and non-phase invariant TS neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited anatomical study and the observed heterogeneity of TS neurons.

claim: Phase invariant TS neurons would give information that a chirp has occurred while non-phase invariant TS neurons would instead transmit contextual information about this chirp.
source: Phase invariant TS neurons would then give information that a chirp has occurred while non-phase invariant TS neurons would instead transmit contextual information about this chirp.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional roles of different TS neuron types.

claim: It is likely that information transmitted by non-phase invariant TS neurons is behaviorally relevant.
source: While our behavioral results do not demonstrate whether the animal can actually perceive information transmitted by non-phase invariant TS neurons, it is likely that this information is behaviorally relevant.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the fact that these neurons project to higher brain areas.

claim: ON and OFF-type cells have been observed across species and sensory modalities.
source: We note that ON and OFF-type cells have been observed across species and sensory modalities (Wassle et al., 1981a; Wassle et al., 1981b; Wassle, 2004; Chalasani et al., 2007; Scholl et al., 2010; Gallio et al., 2011; Frank et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies across different systems.

claim: Downstream neurons receive excitatory inputs from both ON and OFF-type cells.
source: and, further, that downstream neurons receive excitatory inputs from both cell types (Fairhall et al., 2006; Gollisch and Meister, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The discovered computations for generating and refining phase invariance uncovered in the electrosensory system are likely to be applicable to other systems.
source: Thus, the discovered computations for generating and refining phase invariance uncovered in the electrosensory system that involve decoding correlated activity through ON and OFF-type neurons and their subsequent combination are also likely to be applicable.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings based on the ubiquity of ON and OFF-type cells.

claim: The discovered computations are particularly applicable to the primary visual cortex.
source: This is particularly the case in the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability to a specific system.

claim: Simple cells in visual cortex respond selectively to spatial phase.
source: Indeed, while simple cells respond selectively (Movshon, 1975), complex cells instead display responses that are invariant to the spatial phase of a drifting grating (Movshon et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual cortex supported by citations.

claim: Complex cells in visual cortex display responses that are invariant to the spatial phase of a drifting grating.
source: Indeed, while simple cells respond selectively (Movshon, 1975), complex cells instead display responses that are invariant to the spatial phase of a drifting grating (Movshon et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual cortex supported by citations.

claim: It is thought that spatial phase invariance in complex cells arises, at least in part, through integration of input from multiple ON and OFF-type simple cells.
source: It is thought that this invariance arises, at least in part, through integration of input from multiple ON and OFF-type simple cells (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Martinez and Alonso, 2003).
evidence: This is a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: It is conceivable that correlated activity from simple cells could convey a spatial phase invariant representation that is then exploited by complex cells.
source: It is thus conceivable that correlated activity from simple cells could convey a spatial phase invariant representation that is then exploited by complex cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the analogy to the electrosensory system findings.

claim: Correlations between the activities of neighboring neurons are observed ubiquitously in the brain.
source: Further, correlations between the activities of neighboring neurons are observed ubiquitously in the brain (Averbeck et al., 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Correlations between neural activities are dynamically regulated by several factors such as attention, behavioral state, and stimulus statistics.
source: and are dynamically regulated by several factors such as attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009), behavioral state (Vaadia et al., 1995), and stimulus statistics (Chacron and Bastian, 2008; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2012; Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2013; Simmonds and Chacron, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have found that correlated but not single neuron activity can carry information about stimulus attributes.
source: Previous studies have found that correlated but not single neuron activity can carry information about stimulus attributes (deCharms and Merzenich, 1996; Ishikane et al., 2005; Metzen et al., 2015a; Metzen et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Correlated neural activity can mediate the emergence of a neural representation of behaviorally relevant stimuli that is phase invariant.
source: Here, we have instead shown that correlated neural activity can mediate the emergence of a neural representation of behaviorally relevant stimuli that is phase invariant.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Noise correlations were negligible in electroreceptor afferents.
source: We also note that, since previous studies have shown that noise correlations were negligible in electroreceptor afferents (Chacron et al., 2005b; Metzen et al., 2015b), our results focus on signal correlations that give rise to feature invariant representations of natural communication stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The results focus on signal correlations that give rise to feature invariant representations of natural communication stimuli.
source: We also note that, since previous studies have shown that noise correlations were negligible in electroreceptor afferents (Chacron et al., 2005b; Metzen et al., 2015b), our results focus on signal correlations that give rise to feature invariant representations of natural communication stimuli.
evidence: This is a clarification about the type of correlations studied.

claim: Noise correlations are dynamically regulated by stimulus attributes.
source: Nevertheless, noise correlations are also dynamically regulated by stimulus attributes (Chacron and Bastian, 2008) and thus might provide information about sensory input.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Noise correlations might provide information about sensory input.
source: Nevertheless, noise correlations are also dynamically regulated by stimulus attributes (Chacron and Bastian, 2008) and thus might provide information about sensory input.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the dynamic regulation of noise correlations.

claim: The natural communication stimuli considered can be seen as high frequency transients that must be distinguished from a low frequency background (the beat).
source: Finally, we note that the natural communication stimuli considered here can be seen as high frequency transients that must be distinguished from a low frequency background (i.e. the beat).
evidence: This is a characterization of the stimulus structure.

claim: The results are likely applicable to the problem of separating a fast moving object from a slow moving background in the visual system.
source: Thus, it is very likely that our results will be applicable to the problem of separating a fast moving object from a slow moving background as in the visual system (Olveczky et al., 2003)
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability to other systems based on analogous computational problems.

claim: The results are likely applicable to separating a high frequency transient sound occurring simultaneously with a low-frequency background in the auditory system.
source: or to separating a high frequency transient sound occurring simultaneously with a low-frequency background in the auditory system (Berti, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability to other systems based on analogous computational problems.

claim: The electrosensory system exploits the fact that correlated peripheral neuron activity provides an invariant representation through decoding synchronized excitation and inhibition by ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons, respectively.
source: Our results show that this system exploits the fact that correlated peripheral neuron activity provides an invariant representation through decoding synchronized excitation and inhibition by ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Midbrain neurons receiving input from both ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons displayed the most invariant responses.
source: Midbrain neurons receiving input from both ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons displayed the most invariant responses and likely provide a neural correlate of the invariant perception seen at the organismal level.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Midbrain neurons receiving input from both ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons likely provide a neural correlate of the invariant perception seen at the organismal level.
source: Midbrain neurons receiving input from both ON and OFF-type ELL pyramidal neurons displayed the most invariant responses and likely provide a neural correlate of the invariant perception seen at the organismal level.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between neural invariance in TS and behavioral invariance.

claim: All procedures were approved by McGill University's animal care committee under protocol number 5285.
source: All procedures were approved by McGill University's animal care committee under protocol number 5285.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Apteronotus leptorhynchus specimens were acquired from tropical fish suppliers and acclimated to laboratory conditions according to published guidelines.
source: Apteronotus leptorhynchus specimens were acquired from tropical fish suppliers and acclimated to laboratory conditions according to published guidelines (Hitschfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Baseline firing rates for afferents, pyramidal cells, and TS neurons were 380 ± 72 Hz, 12.10 ± 1.74 Hz, and 3.35 ± 3.27 Hz, respectively.
source: Baseline (i.e. in the absence of stimulation) firing rates for afferents, pyramidal cells, and TS neurons were 380 ± 72 Hz, 12.10 ± 1.74 Hz, and 3.35 ± 3.27 Hz.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the recordings.

claim: Baseline firing rates are similar to previously reported values.
source: These are similar to previously reported values (Chacron et al., 2005a; McGillivray et al., 2012; Clarke et al., 2015a; Metzen et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Recordings were only made from neurons that responded to at least one chirp stimulus waveform.
source: We only recorded from neurons that responded to at least one chirp stimulus waveform.
evidence: This is a description of the selection criteria for recorded neurons.

claim: Chirps consisting of Gaussian increases in frequency of 60 Hz and standard deviation of 14 ms were generated on top of a beat with frequency fbeat = 4 Hz.
source: Chirps consisting of Gaussian increases in frequency of 60 Hz and standard deviation of 14 ms, were generated on top of a beat with frequency fbeat = 4 Hz and the resulting AM stimulus waveforms were used as done previously (Vonderschen and Chacron, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus parameters used in the experiments.

claim: The beat phase at which the chirp occurred was systematically varied between 0 and 315 deg in increments of 45 deg.
source: For experimental purposes, we systematically varied the beat phase at which the chirp occurred between 0 and 315 deg in increments of 45 deg, the corresponding AM waveforms (S1 to S8) are shown in Figure 1E.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The chirp rate during a 200 ms window preceding stimulus chirp onset was null (0 ± 0 Hz) after habituation.
source: To measure echo responses to small chirp stimuli delivered at different beat phases, we initially habituated the animal to a 4 Hz beat stimulus lasting 60 s in order to minimize the probability of chirp responses being elicited by the beat alone: the chirp rate during a 200 ms window preceding stimulus chirp onset was null (0 ± 0 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Almost all echo response chirps were classified as type II (98.7%) while the rest were classified as type I (1.3%).
source: Based on this criterion, almost all echo response chirps were classified as type II (98.7%) while the rest were classified as type I (1.3%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral experiments.
